q: Which volcano's slopes grow Nerello Mascalese and Carricante?
exp: Etna's terraces climb to altitudes no other Sicilian zone reaches, on black volcanic soil. The reds come out pale and taut, closer to Nebbiolo than to the island's usual style.

q: Sicily's only DOCG blends Nero d'Avola with a lighter, perfumed red. Which is the partner grape?
exp: Frappato brings red fruit and lift to Nero d'Avola's depth and colour. The wine is Cerasuolo di Vittoria, from the southeast corner of the island.

q: Grenache travelled to Sardinia and is grown there under which name?
exp: Cannonau is the island's signature red, typically warm, herbal and generous in alcohol. Carignano del Sulcis, from old bush vines in the southwest, is the other red to know.

q: Which Sardinian white denomination holds the island's only DOCG rank?
exp: Gallura, in the granite hills of the northeast, gives the most concentrated Vermentino on the island. Vermentino di Sardegna covers the rest of Sardinia at DOC level.

q: A fortified wine from western Sicily is graded Fine, Superiore and Vergine. Which is it?
exp: Marsala was built up by English merchants in the late eighteenth century as a rival to Madeira and Sherry. Its grades turn on ageing, and its colours are oro, ambra and rubino.

q: Which Italian term describes a lightly sparkling wine, held at lower pressure than a fully sparkling one?
exp: Frizzante wines carry roughly one to two and a half atmospheres against three or more for spumante. Lambrusco and Moscato d'Asti are the everyday examples.

q: Zibibbo dried in the sun on a small island south of Sicily makes which sweet wine?
exp: Zibibbo is the local name for Muscat of Alexandria. Pantelleria's relentless wind and heat concentrate the fruit on the vine and on drying racks before pressing.

q: Sweet wines made in Valpolicella and Soave from dried grapes share which name?
exp: Recioto keeps residual sugar because fermentation is halted before the sugar runs out. Amarone is the same dried fruit taken all the way to dryness instead.

q: A number followed by a percentage sign and the letters vol sits near the foot of a European label. What is being stated?
opts: The proportion of the bottle that has been filled
The alcoholic strength as a percentage of volume
The proportion of the named grape in the blend, measured before fermentation
The residual sugar, in grams per litre
exp: The figure is measured on the finished wine, which makes it one of very few numbers on a label describing what is actually in the glass rather than where it came from. Read beside the origin it is also the quickest guide to weight and warmth, which is why a practised buyer looks at it before reading a word of the back label.

q: Beside 75 cl on a European label stands a small lower-case letter e. What does that mark certify?
opts: That the wine is certified organic and may be sold as such anywhere in the European single market
That the wine travelled under a duty suspension
That the fill is controlled as a batch average
That the glass is made from recycled material
exp: The estimated sign belongs to European weights and measures rules: a bottling line is judged on the average contents of a batch, within permitted tolerances, instead of on every individual bottle. It is a metrology mark and says nothing whatever about the wine.

q: A short code such as L3021 is printed on the back label or etched into the glass and appears nowhere else on the bottle. What is it for?
opts: Certifying that the wine passed an official tasting
Naming the vineyard parcel the fruit came from
Recording how many bottles the estate declared to its appellation authority that year
Identifying one bottling run, so a single batch can be traced or withdrawn
exp: Lot marking is a traceability requirement rather than a quality claim, and it is the first thing an authority asks for when a batch has to be recalled. European rules require the letter L in front of the code unless the code is already plainly distinguishable from everything else on the label, and what follows the letter is the bottler's own system.

q: Wine shipped into the United States must identify a business inside the country that a buyer or an inspector can pursue. Which statement carries that?
opts: Product of, followed by the country where the wine was made
Imported by, followed by a company name and address
exp: The importer stands behind the bottle in the market where it is sold, which is why a town in New Jersey or Illinois appears on wines whose producer is world famous. It is commercially useful too: the importer is often the fastest route to the rest of a producer's range.

q: Scanning a square black and white code on a recent European bottle opens the full ingredient list and nutrition table. Which particular must still be printed on the bottle itself?
opts: The names of any fining agents used in the cellar
exp: European rules that reached wine in December 2023 allow the ingredient list and most of the nutrition declaration to live behind an electronic label, but the energy value has to stay on the physical bottle. Allergen information stays printed as well, which is why the sulfite line never migrates to the code.

q: The words mis en bouteille au chateau run in small type along the bottom of a Medoc label. What has the producer committed to?
opts: The wine spent a minimum period in oak before bottling
The wine was bottled at the property that grew and made it
The wine was bottled by hand rather than on a filling line
The wine was bottled within a year of the harvest
exp: This is the French estate-bottling formula, and it ties a single business to the whole chain: it grew the fruit, made the wine and filled the bottle at the address given. It says nothing about how the wine was handled in between or how long it was kept, so it is a statement of responsibility rather than of style or quality.

q: Two German bottles stand side by side, one reading Erzeugerabfullung and the other Gutsabfullung. Which is the tighter claim, and why?
opts: Erzeugerabfullung, which restricts the wine to a single vineyard
Neither; the two words carry identical legal force
Gutsabfullung, which requires an estate working its own vines and a wine-qualified person in charge
Erzeugerabfullung, which requires the bottling to be done inside the village whose name is on the label
exp: Erzeugerabfullung means producer bottling and is broad enough to cover a co-operative filling bottles from a member's fruit. Gutsabfullung is the narrow estate term, so it is the one telling a buyer that the same business farmed the vines and filled the bottle.

q: Along the foot of an Italian label runs the phrase imbottigliato all'origine. What is being claimed?
opts: The wine was bottled in the year of the harvest
The wine was bottled in the zone where it was made, not tankered away and filled elsewhere
The wine was bottled straight from the cask, with neither filtration nor fining before filling
Every grape came from vineyards the bottler owns
exp: Bulk wine can be moved anywhere before it is packaged, and this phrase is the Italian answer to that: the filling was done at the producer's own premises, at a co-operative's, or by a firm inside the denominated zone, and the words are reserved for DOP and IGP wines. They say nothing about who owned the vines, which is the separate claim integralmente prodotto, while a producer wanting to state only who filled the bottle uses imbottigliato da followed by a name.
